Jet.com takes on Amazon for cheaper Internet shopping
checked their site and it seems like some things are a tad cheaper, and others are more expensive. Also, idk if they have free 2-day shipping or not. Sticking with Amazon for now...
I see that Mashable has gotten into the "failing-to-disclose-native-advertising" game.
I welcome the competition but they have a long way to go.

It is simple economics for me. Either I should get the same item for the same price but with other benefits (faster shipping), or everything the same (including shipping time) but cheaper. There has to be an incentive to switch. Maybe if they happen to have that exact item I want that is not sold on the "other" site, but what are the statistical chances with the enormous inventory the other site has?

This. Or, they could come up with some service or product for which my willingness-to-pay increases. Though, what and how that will be, especially in the e-tailing business, is a bit of a red herring.

I placed my first order yesterday on jet.com. "Stacking" your purchases seems to make the biggest difference. For example, if you look up Nivea for Men Active 3 Body Wash - 16.9 Ounce, you should see that it's $3.97, the same as Amazon at the moment. However, they then take 41 cents off of that. If you then waive the right to return the item, they'll take another 8 cents off. You do that once it's in the cart. But if you then change the quantity to 3, it will take $2.94 off, or 98 cents from each item. It's then 24 cents off to waive the return right, so that doesn't scale the same.

By using that strategy I saved a bit on some Quest bars, cat food , dog treats, and some artificial sweetener. It was at least $15 cheaper than amazon, and I used a code to change from a 3 month to 1 year free subscription.

I have no problem buying in bulk to save more. I think that's what makes them the "Costco of the Internet".

$35 is the minimum for free shipping. $49 yearly fee after my first year, so we'll see...

I've received 1 part of the 6 items I ordered so far, so Amazon wins in the shipping department. The remainder is shipping from Nevada, and it supposedly left on Monday but it's only made it Reno, NV to Henderson, CO in the days since. So it'll be 5 days if it makes it by the Saturday stated on the FedEx site.

Not sure if the shipping time is worth the difference in shipping, at least on things you need right away or within a few days.

This all seems very Orwellian to me.. and it reminds me of what Ben Franklin said:

"They that can give up essential liberty to obtain a little temporary safety deserve neither liberty nor safety.” ”Those Who Sacrifice Liberty For Security Deserve Neither.” ”He who would trade liberty for some temporary security, deserves neither liberty nor security.”

..except, in this case, Clark is proposing to give up the liberty of others.

”Those Who Sacrifice Liberty For Security Deserve Neither.”

Can we pause for a moment and recognize how idiotic that is? The entire idea of a social contract is that you give up some freedoms for safety.

I give up my freedom to drive on the left side of the road or to run red lights or speed to ensure that I am safe in from other drivers when driving. Those that violate the directive are punished by the government to help promote safety.

I give up my freedom to settle disputes with physical aggression in order to receive government protection from violence.

The government prohibits people from private ownership of nuclear weapons to make sure no private entity uses one on the populace.

These are examples of freedoms that are good to give up to ensure safety. At some point, we draw a line and say what freedoms we're not willing to give up. In some ways, that line is arbitrary (For example, for weapons, few would argue that private people should get nukes. Or anti-aircraft missiles. But when we get into things like rifles capable of taking down an aircraft, it gets iffy). The line is also movable as cultures shift. The Bill of Rights is one example of such a line. But by the will of the people, the line can be moved in either direction.

Giving up liberty for security is the very basis of a non-anarchic society. To abide by this saying would mean returning to a state of nature.
